title: Micro-organisms & the chain of infection
blurb: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and prions, how they spread in a dental surgery, and how every control you use breaks a link in the chain.
question: A patient with hepatitis B feels perfectly well and has not mentioned it on their medical history. During treatment, the dentist uses an ultrasonic scaler and you are clearing a used local anaesthetic needle. Which routes could spread infection here, and why do you treat every patient the same way?

teach.body: Micro-organisms are living things too small to see without a microscope. Most are harmless, and many live on our skin and in our mouths. The ones that cause disease are called pathogens. A dental surgery brings together blood, saliva, sharp instruments and spray from handpieces, so pathogens have plenty of chances to pass between patients and staff. Everything you do in infection control is designed to stop that happening.

head: Type
What it is
Dental examples
rows: Single cells; divide in two; some form spores
Strep. mutans (caries), Staph. aureus, TB, Legionella
Tiny; multiply only inside living cells
Hepatitis B and C, HIV, herpes simplex, flu
teach.caption: Antibiotics treat bacteria only. Viruses need antivirals or vaccines, and fungi need antifungals such as nystatin or miconazole.

teach.h: Some are much harder to kill than others
teach.body: Bacteria can survive harsh conditions by forming spores, tough resting forms that resist heat and chemicals. Prions are harder still: they are proteins rather than living cells, and they can survive normal decontamination. That is why sterilisation (which kills all micro-organisms, including spores) is used for instruments, and why UK guidance treats endodontic files as single-use. Disinfection only reduces the number of micro-organisms, and cleaning removes the debris they hide in.

bands.label: Enveloped viruses (HIV, flu): easiest to kill

teach.caption: Sterilisation is aimed at the top of this list: if it kills spores, it kills everything below them.
Infection only happens if every link is in place. Remove one, and the chain is broken.

teach.h: Reading the chain in a dental surgery
teach.body: The agent might be hepatitis B. The reservoir is where it lives: an infected patient (who may feel well), contaminated water or a dirty surface. It leaves through a portal of exit such as blood, saliva or a cough. It travels by a mode of transmission, then gets in through a portal of entry: a needlestick, a cut, the eyes, mouth or nose. Finally it needs a susceptible host, someone without immunity, such as an unvaccinated nurse.

children.label: Contact
children.sub: Direct: touching blood or a cold sore. Indirect: via hands, instruments, surfaces

children.label: Through the air
children.sub: Droplets from coughs and spatter; aerosols from handpieces and scalers

children.label: Inoculation
children.sub: Sharps injury, or a splash onto broken skin, eyes or mouth

teach.caption: Blood-borne viruses (hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV) are spread mainly by inoculation.

teach.text: Don't confuse disinfection with sterilisation. Disinfection reduces micro-organisms but may leave spores behind; only sterilisation kills all micro-organisms, including spores. And remember: antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

items: Pathogens are micro-organisms that cause disease: bacteria, viruses, fungi and prions.
Spores and prions are the hardest to destroy; prions may survive decontamination.
Six links: agent, reservoir, portal of exit, transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host.
Routes: contact (direct and indirect), droplet and aerosol, inoculation.
Every control you use (PPE, hand hygiene, vaccination, sterilising) breaks a link.

summary: You can now describe the four types of micro-organism and how hard each is to kill, name the six links in the chain of infection, recognise the routes of transmission in a dental surgery, and explain how infection control measures break the chain.

A.q: A patient has oral thrush under their upper denture. Which type of micro-organism causes this?
A.why: Oral thrush and denture stomatitis are usually caused by Candida albicans, a yeast, which is a type of fungus.

whyNot.0: Bacteria cause caries and gum disease, but thrush is a fungal infection.
whyNot.1: Viruses cause conditions such as cold sores and hepatitis, not thrush.
whyNot.3: Prions cause CJD, a brain disease, not oral thrush.

A.q: The dentist tells a patient that antibiotics will not help their cold sore. Why not?
A.why: Cold sores are caused by the herpes simplex virus. Antibiotics act on bacteria and have no effect on viruses.

whyNot.1: Herpes simplex is a virus, not a fungus.
whyNot.2: Cold sores are not caused by bacteria at all, so spores are irrelevant.
whyNot.3: Antibiotics treat many bacterial infections, not just gum disease; the point is that they don't act on viruses.

A.q: Which link in the chain of infection is broken when a dental nurse is vaccinated against hepatitis B?
A.why: Vaccination gives the nurse immunity, so they are no longer a susceptible host for the virus.

whyNot.0: The portal of exit is how the virus leaves the infected person, which the nurse's vaccine doesn't change.
whyNot.1: The reservoir is the infected patient, who is unaffected by the nurse's vaccination.
whyNot.2: The virus itself still exists; vaccination protects the person, not the agent.

B.q: Which statement about viruses is correct?
options: They are killed by a course of penicillin
They multiply only inside host cells
B.why: Viruses are not cells; they can only multiply by taking over the cells of a living host.

whyNot.0: Penicillin is an antibiotic and has no effect on viruses.
whyNot.2: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.
whyNot.3: Spore formation is a feature of some bacteria, not viruses.

B.q: During an ultrasonic scale, fine particles of water, saliva and blood are released into the air and can be breathed in. Which route of transmission is this?
B.why: Handpieces and ultrasonic scalers create aerosols: tiny particles that hang in the air and can be inhaled.

whyNot.0: Direct contact means touching the source, such as blood or a lesion.
whyNot.1: Inoculation means micro-organisms entering through the skin, for example from a needlestick.
whyNot.2: Ingestion means swallowing contaminated material, not breathing it in.

B.q: Why are endodontic files treated as single-use in UK dental practice?
options: They cannot fit inside an autoclave
B.why: Prions resist normal decontamination, and files are very hard to clean, so UK guidance treats them as single-use.

whyNot.0: Files can wear, but the reason for single use is the prion risk, not blunting.
whyNot.1: Files can physically be sterilised; size is not the issue.
whyNot.3: Spores don't cause rust; and spores are killed by sterilisation, whereas prions may not be.

C.q: A patient tells you they carry hepatitis B but feel completely well. In the chain of infection, the patient is acting as the:
C.why: The reservoir is where the infectious agent lives and multiplies. A carrier who feels well is still a reservoir.

whyNot.1: A portal of entry is how the agent gets into a new host, such as a needlestick wound.
whyNot.2: The susceptible host is the person who might catch the infection, not the carrier.
whyNot.3: The mode of transmission is how the agent travels, such as a sharps injury or splash.

C.q: Which of these is the hardest to destroy by standard decontamination methods?
C.why: Prions are abnormal proteins that resist heat and chemicals and may survive normal decontamination.

whyNot.0: Influenza is an enveloped virus, among the easiest micro-organisms to kill.
whyNot.1: Staph. aureus is a bacterium that is killed by disinfection and sterilisation.
whyNot.3: Candida is a yeast that is killed by standard decontamination.

C.q: A dentist develops an infected finger after examining a patient's active cold sore without gloves. Which route of transmission is this?
C.why: The virus passed straight from the lesion to the dentist's skin by touch, which is direct contact.

whyNot.0: Airborne spread involves droplets or aerosols, not touching a lesion.
whyNot.3: Indirect contact involves an object or surface in between, such as an instrument.

reteach.title: Infection as a line of dominoes
reteach.question: Picture six dominoes in a row. If you pull out any one, the rest can't fall. How does that help you understand infection control?

blocks.body: For someone to catch an infection, six things must line up: a germ, somewhere for it to live, a way out, a way to travel, a way in, and a person who can catch it. Infection control is simply the art of pulling dominoes out of the line. You don't have to remove all six. Removing any one stops the chain, and good practice removes several at once for safety.

blocks.h: Each link and how you break it

steps.label: Portal of entry
steps.sub: PPE; cover cuts with waterproof dressings

blocks.text: A patient who feels well can still be a reservoir. You can't tell who carries a blood-borne virus, so the same precautions are used for every patient.

explain.body: Bacteria are single cells that divide in two and are treated with antibiotics. Viruses are smaller, can only multiply inside living cells, and are not affected by antibiotics. Fungi include yeasts such as Candida, which causes thrush.

explain.caption: Prions are a fourth type: infectious proteins that cause CJD.

test.q: Which type of micro-organism divides in two and can be treated with antibiotics?
test.why: Bacteria reproduce by dividing in two, and antibiotics are designed to kill or stop them.

whyNot.0: Viruses multiply inside host cells and are not affected by antibiotics.
whyNot.1: Prions are proteins, not cells, and antibiotics don't affect them.
whyNot.2: Fungi are treated with antifungals, not antibiotics.

explain.body: Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Each control measure in the surgery targets at least one link.

test.q: You cover a small cut on your hand with a waterproof dressing before clinic. Which link are you breaking?
test.why: Broken skin is a way in for micro-organisms. Covering it closes that portal of entry.

whyNot.0: The reservoir is where the agent lives, such as an infected patient.
whyNot.2: The dressing doesn't destroy the micro-organism itself.
whyNot.3: The portal of exit is how the agent leaves its source, not how it enters you.

explain.body: Contact can be direct (touching blood or a lesion) or indirect (through hands, instruments or surfaces). Droplets and aerosols travel through the air. Inoculation means entry through the skin or mucous membranes, as with a needlestick or a splash.

test.q: A used instrument is put down on a clean worktop, and the next patient's tray is later laid out on the same spot. Which route could spread infection?
test.why: Micro-organisms pass via a contaminated surface to the next patient's instruments: that is indirect contact.

whyNot.1: Airborne spread is through droplets or aerosols, not a surface.
whyNot.2: Direct contact means touching the source itself, with nothing in between.
whyNot.3: Inoculation means entry through broken skin or mucous membranes, such as a needlestick.

explain.body: Cleaning removes debris. Disinfection reduces the number of micro-organisms but may not kill spores. Sterilisation kills all micro-organisms, including spores. Prions may survive even this, which is why some items are single-use.

test.q: Which process kills all micro-organisms, including bacterial spores?
test.why: Sterilisation is the only process that destroys all micro-organisms, including spores.

whyNot.0: Cleaning removes debris but does not reliably kill micro-organisms.
whyNot.1: Disinfection reduces micro-organisms but may not kill spores.
whyNot.3: Hand hygiene reduces micro-organisms on skin; it doesn't sterilise.
